html:
In the winter of 1877 to 1878 several thousand Dungans, Chinese-speaking Muslims also called Hui, fled over the Tian Shan into the Russian Empire after the defeat of their revolt against the Qing. They settled in the Chüy valley of today's Kyrgyzstan and in southern Kazakhstan.

The Dungan revolt began in 1862 in Shaanxi and Gansu and spread to Xinjiang, where Yakub Beg set up his own state in Kashgaria. Qing armies under Zuo Zongtang crushed it with great slaughter. The last rebels, led by Bai Yanhu, crossed the passes in bitter cold, and many died on the way. More Dungans followed in the early 1880s, when Russia handed the Ili region back to China under the Treaty of Saint Petersburg (1881).

Their descendants, around 100,000 people today, still speak a form of northwestern Chinese, written in the Cyrillic alphabet, and keep their own villages, food and customs. They are among the few Chinese speakers who write their language in letters, not characters. Compare the Kyrgyz flight to China in 1916, a movement the other way.
